                    "inherited mapping probe failed: {} absent at {:?}",
                    label,
                    level
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
            Err(error) => {
                kprintln!("inherited mapping probe failed: {}: {:?}", label, error);
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        if translation.physical_address != expected_physical {
            kprintln!(
                "inherited mapping probe failed: {} {:#018x} mapped to {:#018x}, expected {:#018x}",
                label,
                virtual_address,
                translation.physical_address,
                expected_physical
            );
            halt_forever();
        }
        if let Some(first) = first_translation {
            permissions_uniform &= translation.permissions == first.permissions;
            pat_index_uniform &= translation.pat_index == first.pat_index;
        } else {
            first_translation = Some(translation);
        }
        pages += 1;
        offset += rustix_kernel::paging::PAGE_SIZE;
    }
    if let Some(first) = first_translation {
        kprintln!(
            "inherited mapping probe passed: {} ({} pages), first permissions={:?}, PAT index={}, leaf size={}, uniform permissions={}, uniform PAT index={}",
            label,
            pages,
            first.permissions,
            first.pat_index,
            first.page_size,
            permissions_uniform,
            pat_index_uniform
        );
    }
}

#[cfg(feature = "probe-hhdm-frame")]
fn verify_kernel_cache_aliases(
    boot_info: &boot::BootInfo,
    reader: &impl rustix_kernel::paging::PageTableReader<
        Error = rustix_kernel::memory::HhdmAddressError,
    >,
    root: rustix_kernel::paging::Cr3Root,
    config: rustix_kernel::paging::PageWalkConfig,
    pat: rustix_kernel::paging::PatLayout,
    mtrrs: &rustix_kernel::paging::ValidatedMtrrLayout,
    label: &str,
    kernel_virtual_start: u64,
    physical_start: u64,
    length: u64,
) {
    use rustix_kernel::paging::{walk_virtual_address, PageWalkOutcome};

    let mut offset = 0;
    let mut pages = 0;
    while offset < length {
        let physical = match physical_start.checked_add(offset) {
            Some(address) => address,
            None => {
                kprintln!("cache-alias probe failed: {} physical overflow", label);
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        let kernel_virtual = match kernel_virtual_start.checked_add(offset) {
            Some(address) => address,
            None => {
                kprintln!("cache-alias probe failed: {} virtual overflow", label);
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        let hhdm_virtual = match boot_info.memory_map.limine_hhdm_address(
            boot_info.hhdm_offset,
            physical,
            rustix_kernel::paging::PAGE_SIZE,
            boot_info.cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
            boot_info.cpu_info.active_linear_address_bits,
        ) {
            Ok(address) => address,
            Err(error) => {
                kprintln!(
                    "cache-alias probe failed: {} HHDM range: {:?}",
                    label,
                    error
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        let kernel_translation = match walk_virtual_address(reader, root, kernel_virtual, config) {
            Ok(PageWalkOutcome::Mapped(translation)) => translation,
            result => {
                kprintln!(
                    "cache-alias probe failed: {} kernel walk: {:?}",
                    label,
                    result
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        let hhdm_translation = match walk_virtual_address(reader, root, hhdm_virtual, config) {
            Ok(PageWalkOutcome::Mapped(translation)) => translation,
            result => {
                kprintln!(
                    "cache-alias probe failed: {} HHDM walk: {:?}",
                    label,
                    result
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        if kernel_translation.physical_address != physical
            || hhdm_translation.physical_address != physical
        {
            kprintln!(
                "cache-alias probe failed: {} physical {:#018x} has inconsistent translations",
                label,
                physical
            );
            halt_forever();
        }
        let kernel_type = match mtrrs.effective_memory_type_for(
            physical,
            pat,
            kernel_translation.pat_index,
            boot_info.cpu_info.normal_caching,
        ) {
            Ok(memory_type) => memory_type,
            Err(error) => {
                kprintln!(
                    "cache-alias probe failed: {} kernel PAT/MTRR: {:?}",
                    label,
                    error
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        let hhdm_type = match mtrrs.effective_memory_type_for(
            physical,
            pat,
            hhdm_translation.pat_index,
            boot_info.cpu_info.normal_caching,
        ) {
            Ok(memory_type) => memory_type,
            Err(error) => {
                kprintln!(
                    "cache-alias probe failed: {} HHDM PAT/MTRR: {:?}",
                    label,
                    error
                );
                halt_forever();
            }
        };
        if kernel_type != hhdm_type {
            kprintln!(
                "cache-alias conflict: {} PA {:#018x}, kernel {:?} vs HHDM {:?}",
                label,
                physical,
                kernel_type,
                hhdm_type
            );
            halt_forever();
        }
        pages += 1;
        offset += rustix_kernel::paging::PAGE_SIZE;
    }
    kprintln!(
        "cache-alias probe passed: {} ({} pages; effective types match)",
        label,
        pages
    );
}

fn release_probe_frame(
    allocator: &mut rustix_kernel::frame::FrameAllocator,
    frame: rustix_kernel::frame::Frame,
) {
    if let Err(error) = allocator.deallocate(frame) {
        kprintln!(
            "HHDM frame probe failed to return its frame: {:?}",
            error.error
        );
        halt_forever();
    }
}

#[cfg(feature = "inject-page-fault")]
fn run_fault_injection() {
    kprintln!("fault injection: triggering page fault at 0x00000000deadbeef");
    // SAFETY: This is an opt-in QEMU test that deliberately reads an unmapped
    // low virtual address; the installed page-fault handler is expected to halt.
    unsafe {
        core::arch::asm!(
            "mov rax, 0xdeadbeef",
            "mov rax, qword ptr [rax]",
            out("rax") _,
            options(nostack)
        );
    }
    kprintln!("fault injection unexpectedly returned");
    halt_forever();
}

#[cfg(feature = "inject-invalid-opcode")]
fn run_fault_injection() {
    kprintln!("fault injection: triggering invalid opcode with ud2");
    // SAFETY: This is an opt-in QEMU test that deliberately raises #UD; the
    // installed invalid-opcode handler is expected to halt.
    unsafe { core::arch::asm!("ud2", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    kprintln!("fault injection unexpectedly returned");
    halt_forever();
}

#[cfg(feature = "inject-general-protection")]
fn run_fault_injection() {
    kprintln!("fault injection: triggering general protection with invalid DS selector");
    // SAFETY: The selector index is outside the installed GDT limit, so loading
    // it into DS deliberately raises a kernel-origin #GP in QEMU.
    unsafe {
        core::arch::asm!(
            "mov ax, 0xffff",
            "mov ds, ax",
            out("ax") _,
            options(nostack)
        )
    };
    kprintln!("fault injection unexpectedly returned");
    halt_forever();
}

#[cfg(feature = "inject-divide-error")]
fn run_fault_injection() {
    kprintln!("fault injection: triggering divide error with a zero divisor");
    // SAFETY: Integer division by zero deliberately raises kernel-origin #DE.
    unsafe {
        core::arch::asm!(
            "xor edx, edx",
            "xor eax, eax",
            "xor ecx, ecx",
            "div ecx",
            out("eax") _,
            out("edx") _,
            out("ecx") _,
            options(nostack)
        )
    };
    kprintln!("fault injection unexpectedly returned");
    halt_forever();
}

/// Set once the fatal panic path has started. A panic from inside the fatal
/// path stops silently instead of recursively printing or looping diagnostics.
static FATAL_PANIC_ACTIVE: core::sync::atomic::AtomicBool =
    core::sync::atomic::AtomicBool::new(false);

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(info: &PanicInfo<'_>) -> ! {
    // Mask maskable interrupts before any diagnostics run: another kernel
    // thread must not resume after a panic is declared, and the fatal report
    // must not be preempted mid-print.
    //
    // SAFETY: Kernel panic path runs at CPL 0; masking IF is always sound.
    unsafe { core::arch::asm!("cli", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    if FATAL_PANIC_ACTIVE.swap(true, core::sync::atomic::Ordering::Acquire) {
        loop {
            // SAFETY: Re-entrant panics are deliberately silent.
            unsafe { core::arch::asm!("cli; hlt", options(nomem, nostack)) };
        }
    }
    arch::x86_64::serial::initialize();
    kprintln!("KERNEL PANIC: {}", info);
    halt_forever()
}

fn halt_forever() -> ! {
    loop {
        // SAFETY: The bootstrap has no interrupt handlers or scheduler to resume.
        unsafe { core::arch::asm!("cli; hlt", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    }
}

# Unix-like process and syscall direction

**Status: bounded single-vCPU Milestone 4 implementation validated.** Default boot launches a controlled Ring 3 `rustix-init`; the process smoke additionally exercises generation-safe slot reuse, child-originated nested spawn, orphan cleanup, and append-only `exec` (syscall 11). Spawn copies a bounded ELF image into kernel-owned staging before returning, prepares a private root, guard, and 1–16-page zeroed stack, then publishes a cooperative task. The QEMU smokes validate process teardown, status-copyout retry, exec replacement and old-image reclamation, and malformed syscall-return termination. The runtime remains deliberately bounded to four concurrent processes, cooperative with IF disabled, and single-vCPU. General-purpose process scheduling, curated kernel mappings, SMP, and physical-hardware validation remain future work.

Rustix aims to expose a small, versioned syscall surface that can support Unix-like processes and tools. The kernel must own this interface rather than inherit an ABI accidentally from a bootloader or emulator.

## Proposed compatibility principles

- Processes have independent virtual address spaces and explicit lifecycle states.
- File descriptors are per-process integer handles to kernel-managed objects; descriptor inheritance, close-on-exec, duplication, and sharing semantics must be specified together.
- Syscalls use one documented error convention and stable numeric identifiers. New operations must not silently repurpose old numbers.
- Arguments crossing privilege boundaries are copied or validated using narrowly scoped helpers. `ProcessAddressSpaceRoots::copy_from_user` and `copy_to_user` preflight the complete lower-half mapped range, check writable metadata for kernel-to-user copies, and operate only on owned frame tokens through `UserFrameMemory`; they never form a Rust reference from a user virtual address. Backend copy faults report the completed prefix. The diagnostic user-exception path terminates a process on supported CPL3 faults; it does not make arbitrary kernel memory accesses recoverable.
- Blocking, interruption, cancellation, and restart behavior are explicit for each syscall class.
- A compatibility layer (for example, POSIX-shaped libc behavior) remains separate from internal kernel APIs.

## Initial syscall ABI v1 contract (specified; register decoding implemented)

ABI version `1.1` is identified by `abi_version()`, syscall number `0`, returning `0x0001_0001` in `RAX`. In v1, `RAX` returns a signed 64-bit result: nonnegative values are success (including byte counts, addresses, and PIDs); errors are negative stable error numbers. ABI versioning is append-only: existing syscall numbers, argument meanings, layouts, and error values never change or get reused. There is no POSIX compatibility claim. `src/syscall.rs` implements stable number/error constants, request decoding, and the assembly-matched syscall context layout. The `crates/rustix-user` crate provides typed `no_std` wrappers, including bounded `spawn` and `exec`, plus process entry, I/O, formatting, panic, and optional mmap-backed allocation helpers; host tests cover decoding, wrapper limits, I/O formatting, and allocator behavior. The diagnostic process runtime implements the calls listed below. Init can spawn up to three children from user-memory ELF images; the kernel copies each complete bounded image before returning, so the source can be unmapped immediately. Spawn prepares the child root before publishing its context to a pre-reserved cooperative task. Wait blocks the caller while a matching child runs and resumes to copy status, reclaim the inactive child root, then reap. The QEMU smoke validates three children, malformed-image and invalid-source rejection, a two-page zeroed child stack, task-capacity exhaustion, source unmapping before child execution, status-copyout retry, per-child root reclamation, and final teardown. This is bounded diagnostic support, not default-boot userspace or general-purpose process scheduling.

| Number | Call | Register arguments | Result / behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `abi_version` | none | `0x0001_0001` (major 1, minor 1). |
| 1 | `exit` | `RDI`: signed 32-bit status in the low 32 bits (upper bits ignored) | Does not return; status is retained exactly by the parent wait record. |
| 2 | `write` | `RDI`: fd, `RSI`: user buffer, `RDX`: byte length | Returns bytes accepted; a short positive result is valid. Initial descriptors 1 and 2 are stdout/stderr console streams; other descriptors return `-EBADF`. Maximum request is 4096 bytes; zero length returns 0 without validating the pointer. |
| 3 | `wait` | `RDI`: child PID (0 means any child), `RSI`: optional user pointer to signed 32-bit exit status | ABI contract: blocks until a matching child exits and returns its PID. A non-null status output must be writable before the child is reaped; no matching child returns `-ECHILD`. The diagnostic supports already-exited children and its fixed set of kernel-prepared running children, blocking the parent task and scheduling them before resuming. Failed status copyout returns `-EFAULT` without reaping or releasing the child's root; successful copyout is followed by inactive-root teardown and then record reaping. |
| 4 | `mmap` | `RDI`: requested byte length, `1..=4096` | Maps one zero-filled, read/write, non-executable anonymous page and returns its user address. Lengths above one page return `-E2BIG`; the first-fit address comes from the bounded anonymous region window; exhaustion returns `-ENOMEM`. |
| 5 | `munmap` | `RDI`: page-aligned anonymous base, `RSI`: exactly `4096` | Removes one exact page previously allocated by `mmap`; invalid addresses, lengths, or non-anonymous regions return `-EINVAL`. |
| 6 | `close` | `RDI`: descriptor | Closes one process-local descriptor; invalid or already-closed descriptors return `-EBADF`. |
| 7 | `dup` | `RDI`: source descriptor | Duplicates the stream into the lowest free descriptor slot at or above 3; invalid descriptors return `-EBADF`, and the fixed table limit returns `-EMFILE`. |
| 8 | `mmap_region` | `RDI`: requested byte length, `1..=1 MiB` | Maps a contiguous, zero-filled RW/NX anonymous region, rounding length up to 4 KiB. Returns its base; reservation, frame, or page-table exhaustion returns `-ENOMEM`. |
| 9 | `munmap_region` | `RDI`: exact region base, `RSI`: exact page-rounded region length | Unmaps one exact anonymous region returned by `mmap_region`; invalid ranges, lengths, or non-anonymous regions return `-EINVAL`. |
| 10 | `spawn` | `RDI`: user ELF image pointer, `RSI`: image length (`1..=1 MiB`), `RDX`: initial stack pages (`1..=16`) | Copies the complete read-only user range into kernel staging, validates and loads a static ELF64 image into a private root, prepares a guard and zeroed RW/NX stack, and returns the child PID. Invalid pointers return `-EFAULT`; malformed ELF/stack arguments return `-EINVAL`; resource exhaustion returns `-ENOMEM`. Any active process in the controlled runtime may spawn; four process slots (including init) bound concurrent processes. |
| 11 | `exec` | `RDI`: user ELF image pointer, `RSI`: image length (`1..=1 MiB`), `RDX`: initial stack pages (`1..=16`) | Replaces the caller's root, image, and stack with a new static ELF image. On success the syscall does not return; the process resumes Ring 3 at the replacement image's entry with a fresh zeroed stack, preserving PID, descriptors, parent, and children. Malformed images return `-EINVAL`, invalid pointers `-EFAULT`, and resource failures `-ENOMEM`; the original image remains usable. The user x87/SSE state is preserved across a successful exec. |

Numbers above 11 are unassigned and return `-ENOSYS`; assigning a number later is an additive extension, never a reinterpretation. `mmap`, `munmap`, `mmap_region`, `munmap_region`, `spawn`, `close`, and `dup` are available in the controlled process runtime used by the default bundled init; this is not a general application loader. Descriptor 0 is reserved for input but v1 has no `read` or `open` call. Descriptors 1 and 2 start as stdout/stderr; child process records inherit the parent's current console-descriptor table, duplication creates an independent handle to the same stream, and process exit clears its descriptor table. The initial process is created by the kernel loader, not a syscall.

Stable v1 error numbers (returned negated in `RAX`) are: `1 EINVAL`, `2 EBADF`, `3 EFAULT`, `4 ENOMEM`, `5 ECHILD`, `6 EINTR`, `7 EIO`, `8 ENOSYS`, `9 E2BIG`, `10 EOVERFLOW`, `11 ENOTSUP`, and `12 EMFILE`. Unknown syscall numbers return `-ENOSYS`. Pointer-plus-length ranges use checked arithmetic and must lie wholly in a mapped lower-half user range. `write` preflights the whole input range before output; a later endpoint failure may return a short count, and an error before progress returns `-EIO`. A copy fault after progress returns the completed prefix. `mmap`/`mmap_region` provide zeroed RW/NX mappings; multi-page region mapping is bounded to 1 MiB and rolls back on failure. Unmap operations require an exact anonymous reservation, and the kernel releases frames only after removing their PTEs. `spawn` preflights and copies the complete bounded image from the caller through owned frame tokens into fixed kernel staging before ELF parsing; it does not retain the caller pointer. An invalid source returns `-EFAULT`, malformed static ELF or stack layout returns `-EINVAL`, and capacity/resource failures return `-ENOMEM`. `wait` copies optional status before reaping; failed copyout returns `-EFAULT` and leaves the child waitable. The diagnostic blocks the parent task on a process-exit queue when a matching child is running, then resumes and rechecks the requested PID. It supports the fixed pre-reserved task set only; arbitrary process launch/scheduling, interruption, signals, asynchronous delivery, and automatic syscall restart remain future work.

All ABI integers are fixed-width little-endian x86_64 values. The wait status is one signed 32-bit integer with no implicit padding or extra fields. No other user-visible structs exist in v1.

## Initial x86_64 entry design (Milestone 4; diagnostic path integrated)

The bounded single-vCPU process runtime enters Ring 3 with a validated five-word `IRETQ` frame and enters the kernel with `int $0x80` through a dedicated DPL-3 IDT gate. Default boot launches the controlled bundled init; diagnostic QEMU variants exercise additional process and fault cases. This intentionally avoids `SYSCALL`/`SYSRET`, `STAR`/`LSTAR`/`FMASK`, and `SWAPGS` state transitions. The register and error contract below is the versioned v1 ABI, but the syscall surface and runtime are not general-purpose. The `rustix-user` crate includes typed wrappers, the `run_main` process-entry helper, complete-write and allocation-free formatting helpers, best-effort panic reporting, and an optional mmap-backed global allocator. The allocator obtains zeroed pages through `mmap`, serves power-of-two classes from 16 through 2048 bytes, rejects larger or over-aligned requests, and retains pages until process teardown; applications opt in by declaring `UserAllocator` as their global allocator. The runtime also exposes bounded multi-page `mmap_region`/`munmap_region` wrappers, validated by `rustix-init` across a page boundary. `rustix-init` exercises the entry helper and heap with `Vec` and `Box`, but the crate remains an early runtime and is not a general application or process-scheduling environment.

- **Vector ownership:** `0x80` lies inside the device-vector range (`0x20..=0xef`) and is reserved by `InterruptVectorAllocator`; generic IRQ allocation/release cannot claim it. The IDT installs a dedicated DPL-3 interrupt gate rather than the generic device-IRQ stub. Its assembly entry rejects CPL0 invocation, saves all GPRs and x87/SSE state, clears the direction flag, and calls a normalized Rust dispatcher with IF clear. The controlled runtime implements ABI-version discovery, write, exit, anonymous mappings, spawn, wait, and exec. Active processes can create children as distinct cooperative scheduler tasks from copied user images; concurrent process capacity is fixed at four. Per-task TSS entry stacks are allocator-backed, reusable, and reclaimed when tasks are reaped. This remains a bounded runtime, not a general userspace scheduler.
- **Selectors:** the current GDT uses `0x08` for kernel code, `0x10` for kernel data, and `0x18` for the two-slot TSS descriptor. Ring-3 data and 64-bit code descriptors are appended at GDT indexes 5 and 6, with compile-time selector assertions for user data `0x2b` and user code `0x33` (RPL 3); the process probe uses these selectors in its validated entry frame.
- **Privilege stack:** a CPL3-to-CPL0 interrupt uses `TSS.RSP0`. Each process task owns bounded allocator-backed scheduler and TSS entry stacks; the kernel maps them supervisor-only, writable, and NX. `TSS.RSP0` follows the active task. Scheduler-owned stacks are reclaimed after task exit and their bounded slots can be reused. Each `enter_user` call has a separate entry-state record for its saved kernel RSP, exit status, callback context, prior nested entry, and kernel FXSAVE image; the exit trampoline restores the correct record. Process roots share the validated upper-half mappings. After init's exit trampoline returns to the bootstrap stack, the probe restores bootstrap `RSP0`. Init can spawn at most three children, while the static TSS slots and task set impose fixed per-run capacity. Callers must disable local interrupts and guarantee the stack is mapped writable in every address space that can run until the next update. A future SMP design needs per-CPU TSS and entry-stack state.
- **Entry frame and state:** the dedicated assembly stub saves all GPRs in the `SyscallContext` layout, passes the five-word privilege frame separately from the exception frame, and saves/restores x87/SSE state around the Rust dispatcher; AVX remains disabled under the current CPU-state policy. Per-entry records hold continuation RSP, exit state, callback context, the prior nested entry, and kernel FXSAVE state instead of shared depth-indexed globals. The scheduler selects among these records through cooperative task contexts; timer preemption remains disabled while user code runs. Kernel code runs with the direction flag clear. The process probe validates saved RIP/RSP against the active process mappings and accesses user buffers only through owned frame tokens. Spawn copies bytes before publishing a child; wait can block and recheck any matching child in the bounded pre-reserved set. General userspace scheduling is not provided.
- **Initial register convention:** `RAX` carries the syscall number; arguments use `RDI`, `RSI`, `RDX`, `R10`, `R8`, and `R9`; `RAX` carries the result. This convention and its initial numbers/errors are versioned as ABI v1. Implemented operations remain a subset of the documented contract.
- **Return validation:** use `IRETQ`, not `SYSRET`. Initial entry uses a host-tested frame sanitizer that requires exact ring-3 selectors, a canonical lower-half instruction pointer, a lower-half stack range, 16-byte initial stack alignment, and safe flags. Syscall resume uses a separate sanitizer that keeps exact selectors, canonical lower-half address shape, and privileged-flag checks but does not impose 16-byte alignment on an in-function RSP; it replaces user flags with `0x2` (IF remains clear). Once a process is active, the dispatcher also validates the saved instruction pointer against an executable mapping and the saved stack pointer against a writable NX mapping. A malformed frame is converted into process exit rather than returned to CPL3.
- **NMI and interrupt policy:** no GS-base swap is needed on this entry path. NMI, double fault, and machine check remain fatal even when their saved CS indicates CPL3. Other user-origin exceptions terminate the process with status `128 + vector` in the diagnostic runtime; QEMU exercises CPL3 #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE. Kernel-origin #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE are separately tested as fatal. Ordinary maskable IRQs stay disabled throughout user-task execution; scheduler switches occur only at explicit cooperative waits and exits.

This path depends on each process root sharing supervisor-only upper-half mappings that cover syscall/exception code, the IDT, GDT, TSS, and active kernel stacks. The init and spawn-created child roots plus nested syscall/exception transitions are exercised by opt-in QEMU smokes, but the shared Limine-derived kernel mapping is not a curated kernel map or a general isolation policy. Default boot currently launches the controlled init runtime after the bounded lifecycle, wait, and fault/teardown paths are validated. This does not provide general process scheduling or isolation from the shared Limine-derived kernel mapping.

### Process address spaces (design; root construction partially implemented)

Use a separate four- or five-level root per process. The initial source is the retained active clone of Limine's hierarchy, not a curated clean-room root. Each process root owns its root page, all lower-half intermediate tables, and every user leaf frame. Keep the kernel-root owner alive for the lifetime of every process root. Copy only upper-half top-level entries from that owner into each process root; these entries are non-owning references to shared kernel subtrees, not deep copies, and must never be released by a process teardown. Do not copy lower-half entries from the kernel root.

Before publishing a shared kernel subtree, validate its page-table structure and physical bounds and reject any effectively user-accessible leaf. U/S permission is the conjunction of every entry on a path, so a U/S bit on one non-leaf alone does not grant user access. When copying upper-half root entries, clear their U/S bit as defense in depth; a user leaf then cannot become accessible if a lower entry changes. `paging::validate_supervisor_kernel_half` implements the bounded, read-only structural/effective-permission preflight, but it does not install roots or prove physical backing is readable; the supplied reader must provide that access guarantee. Sharing the active clone means every accepted upper-half supervisor mapping and alias is present in every process CR3. This is not a curated kernel map or kernel-page-table isolation, and it provides no transient-execution protection. User mappings remain private to one process, are confined to the lower canonical half, preserve W^X, and are non-global in the first implementation.

The kernel address-space owner is the only authority allowed to modify shared upper-half tables. Mutations must be serialized with local interrupts disabled on the current single-vCPU system and invalidate the affected local translation before the mapping change is relied on. A process root may not edit or reclaim shared tables. `ProcessAddressSpaceRoots::destroy` releases only private user leaves, intermediate tables, and the root; the caller must first switch CR3 to a different live root and invalidate this root's local non-global translations. Keep the shared kernel owner alive. PCID-aware invalidation and SMP shootdown remain unsupported and need a separate design.

The current `CandidatePageTables` deep-clones the inherited hierarchy, tracks all cloned tables as owned, and holds an exclusive mutable borrow of one memory backend; it is not itself the process-address-space abstraction. `SharedKernelHalf` validates and snapshots the sanitized upper root entries while borrowing the kernel owner. `ProcessAddressSpaceRoots` uses one exclusive backend borrow for multiple private roots, maps allocator-owned user 4 KiB leaves only in inactive lower halves, retains writable/executable permission metadata, validates the initial executable entry and writable NX stack, provides range-preflighted copy-in/copy-out through a separate `UserFrameMemory` backend, and destroys private leaf/table/root frames without freeing shared subtrees. Host tests cover four-/five-level sharing, U/S sanitization, independent mappings, permission checks, cross-page copies, unmap ownership, active-root release rejection, and rollback. The default boot path prepares the init root; the process-smoke variant additionally accepts nested child images from user buffers. It copies each image through checked frame tokens before parsing, creates a private root and guarded stack, then publishes a stable callback context to one of the pre-mapped cooperative task slots. Init can wait for a specific child; status copyout precedes reap, and CR3 is restored before kernel wait/reap and teardown. The bounded probe reclaims scheduler-owned task stacks after all tasks exit, but retains PID-indexed static TSS entry stacks and the Limine-derived shared kernel subtree; it is not a default-boot launcher or curated kernel-map policy. Keep the kernel owner alive and immutable for the shared view's lifetime; callers must use a distinct page-table backend for process-owned tables.

### Static ELF64 image validation and page initialization (partial)

`src/elf.rs` parses little-endian x86_64 `ET_EXEC` images without allocation. It bounds the program-header count, load-segment count, and total mapped pages; checks file and virtual arithmetic, page alignment and `p_align` congruence, lower-half canonical ranges, non-overlapping page spans, readable segment flags, W^X, and that the entry point lies in a non-writable executable `PT_LOAD`. It rejects dynamic/interpreter and TLS segments and executable-stack requests. This initial format intentionally requires page-aligned load offsets/addresses and supports at most 64 program headers, 16 load segments, and 64 load pages. `populate_segment_page` copies one load page into an allocator-owned frame through `UserFrameMemory`, zero-filling bytes beyond the file payload. `load_into_process_root` allocates, populates, cache-selects, and maps every load page into an inactive process root. The diagnostic build reproducibly compiles `crates/rustix-init` as a static ELF64 payload; `just process-smoke` loads and runs the normal image, and `just user-fault-smoke` builds a `ud2` entry variant and validates process termination/reaping/teardown.

## ABI decisions still pending beyond v1

The initial v1 versioning, error encoding, syscall numbers, register-level request decoding, and assembly-matched syscall context layout are implemented in `src/syscall.rs`. The `int 0x80` path serves ABI-version, descriptor-authorized write, close/dup, spawn, exec, wait, one-page and multi-page mmap/munmap, and exit calls. Spawn copies a user ELF to bounded kernel staging, prepares its private root and stack, and starts it in a reusable task slot; exec replaces the caller's root, image, and stack while preserving PID, descriptors, parent, and children. The process smoke validates nested spawn, five rounds of bounded slot reuse, orphan cleanup, exec replacement and old-image reclamation, and final frame restoration. The process table and wait path remain fixed-capacity at four concurrent processes; this is not a general process-execution service. The table's console descriptors are not general file objects, and there is no read/open support. User faults terminate a process only while the opt-in callback is installed; QEMU covers CPL3 #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE and kernel-fatal coverage for the same vectors. Still open are general/dynamic task and TSS-stack ownership/reclamation, descriptor-object sharing/close-on-exec, read/open support, wait interruption/signals, clocks, and additional user-visible structure contracts.

## Suggested first user-visible slice

The controlled `no_std` init runs during default boot; opt-in QEMU variants exercise additional fault and process scenarios. It exercises ABI-version discovery, descriptor duplication/write/close, EFAULT, anonymous mappings, `Vec`/`Box`, and syscall 10 spawn with three user-supplied child images. Init unmaps the source buffer immediately after spawn, checks the fourth spawn fails at capacity, waits for each returned PID, retries after a bad status pointer, then exits for kernel-side wait/reap. All three children validate their two-page zeroed stacks, write a marker, and exit with status 7. This demonstrates bounded user-originated process creation and execution, not a general process-execution environment. The runtime includes bounded `exec`, nested spawn, and reusable/reclaimed task entry stacks; arbitrary-capacity process scheduling and general executable services remain future work. Read/open and general descriptor-object semantics need their own implementation and adversarial tests before any Unix-compatibility claim.

# Architecture overview

## Goals

Rustix is a from-scratch operating system project with its own kernel, written in Rust. The intended initial platform is 64-bit x86 (`x86_64`), with a Unix-like process and file-descriptor model. The kernel should eventually own machine initialization, physical and virtual memory management, interrupt handling, scheduling, system calls, and device policy. A bootloader is a transport into the kernel, not a replacement for those facilities.

Unix-like is a compatibility direction. It does **not** mean the current kernel is POSIX-compliant, nor does it commit the project to a particular existing kernel's internals. Compatibility profiles and a userland should be defined only after the underlying process, descriptor, and syscall semantics are implemented and tested.

## Current implementation

1. Cargo builds a `no_std`, `no_main` ELF for `x86_64-unknown-none` and uses Limine for the boot handoff.
2. `_start` initializes COM1 and exception diagnostics, captures a validated boot snapshot and frame-allocator state, activates a clone of Limine's page tables, configures the validated single-vCPU APIC/PIT path, installs bounded heap growth, and starts the shell runtime when timer and UART IRQ setup succeed.
3. Crabshell reads an ASCII command line from COM1's bounded IRQ queue and blocks cooperatively while idle; polling remains fallback. It supports basic navigation, directory creation/listing, and text-file operations.
4. The separately packaged `crabshell` `no_std` crate parses commands without allocation or dependence on kernel I/O, making that layer reusable by a future graphical frontend.
5. The kernel library contains checked memory accounting, bounded ACPI/IRQ/time/input/scheduler policies, heap tests, and the bounded VFS implementation, covered by host-side tests.

The shell and filesystem run in kernel mode. Files exist only in RAM and disappear at reboot. Kernel-origin exceptions remain fatal; an opt-in synchronous Ring 3 diagnostic can terminate a user process on noncritical exceptions, with QEMU coverage for CPL3 #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE. Selected timer/UART/PS/2 IRQ routes are enabled after APIC, IDT, and handler setup. The single-vCPU scheduler supports cooperative waits/yields and PIT-driven preemption; IRQ-safe locking protects the global heap, while IRQ/exception allocation remains prohibited. Timer context switches preserve x87/SSE state with per-context FXSAVE areas. The active page tables are an owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy, with bounded active mapping and a global heap consisting of a 256 KiB BSS arena plus up to 1 MiB of frame-backed growth. The default kernel launches a controlled Ring 3 `rustix-init` through the documented syscall ABI; process execution remains bounded and cooperative, not a general userspace scheduler. There is no clean-room kernel mapping policy, general-purpose MMIO/mapping policy, frame reclamation, SMP, userspace process scheduler, on-disk filesystem, or network stack.

## Intended layers (planned)

```text
User programs and system utilities
        | versioned syscall ABI
Kernel services: processes, descriptors, VFS, IPC, signals
        | explicit ownership and authorization checks
Core kernel: scheduler, virtual memory, physical frames, interrupts
        | narrow architecture abstractions
x86_64 platform: paging, exceptions, timers, AP startup, drivers
        | Limine boot handoff only
Firmware and hardware
```

The diagram is a target decomposition, not a claim that those layers are implemented. Architecture-independent policy should live in safe Rust where possible; privileged instructions and raw device access should stay in small, reviewed architecture modules.

## Design constraints

- **Freestanding:** kernel code does not link `std`; global allocation is bounded, frame-backed growth is explicit, and allocation is forbidden in IRQ/exception context.
- **Explicit unsafe boundaries:** raw pointers from boot protocol responses and x86 port I/O are unsafe. Each use must document its preconditions and remain short-lived.
- **Fail visibly:** early boot failures should produce serial diagnostics where possible and then halt, rather than continue with invalid machine state.
- **Checked arithmetic:** physical ranges, sizes, and address translations must reject overflow.
- **No premature ABI:** userspace interfaces stay unstable until process lifetime, error conventions, copy-in/copy-out, and versioning are designed together.
- **Hardware-independent tests:** parsing, range arithmetic, and policy should be testable as ordinary host-side Rust wherever possible.

## Boot and CPU assumptions

The current target is x86_64, with a 4 KiB page-oriented linker layout and no red zone. Limine performs the initial platform setup required by its protocol. Rustix must not assume that receiving a memory-map response means it owns the loader's page tables or can overwrite reserved regions. The bootstrap enables only validated single-vCPU APIC routes after their handlers and EOI paths are ready; it does not start application processors. Timer preemption is enabled only after the scheduler runtime is live.

See [Boot protocol](boot.md), [Memory management](memory.md), [x86_64 drivers](drivers.md), [Crabshell](crabshell.md), and [the roadmap](../roadmap/README.md) for subsystem boundaries and planned acceptance criteria.

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side ACPI parser/traversal, borrowed-page mapping, IRQ vector allocator, PIT rate/time arithmetic, SPSC input-queue wraparound, scheduler, process lifecycle, descriptor-table and user-region policy, reusable ELF/root/guard/stack preparation, injected rollback, process-root/mapping/private-table metadata exhaustion with ownership-preserving failures, and frame-exhaustion rollback at every sub-success remaining-frame budget, syscall request decoding, memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, heap, RAM-filesystem, Crabshell parser, and `rustix-user` syscall decoding, short-write, and formatting tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO (including the static `rustix-init` ELF payload), boot it in QEMU's default BIOS mode, require the kernel to parse/validate the bundled init entry and load-page count, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.
5. `just uefi-smoke` — boot the same ISO with OVMF and require the copied MADT report, CR3/page-table transition and TLB-flush markers, timer IRQ delivery/EOI, and shell prompt within a deadline.
6. `just active-map-smoke` and `just thread-smoke` — exercise active owned-page mapping/TLB invalidation and (under OVMF) IRQ-save lock IF restoration, cooperative event/wait behavior, timer preemption of non-yielding workers, x87/SSE state preservation, timed sleep while another ready thread repeatedly yields, guarded stacks, and frame-backed heap growth; both restore the default image.
7. `just input-smoke` — under OVMF, type a partial `pwd` over UART, inject ordinary and extended PS/2 scancodes through QMP, require each diagnostic to redraw the prompt and partial line, then finish the command and verify its output. The QMP socket is created under the host temporary directory because WSL `/mnt/c` does not support Unix sockets.
8. `just fault-smoke`, `just process-smoke`, and `just user-fault-smoke` — verify fatal kernel #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE diagnostics, then run bundled init in a diagnostic Ring 3 root. The process variant checks a fresh initial-stack byte, ABI version, formatted output, dup/write/close including `-EBADF`, zero-filled RW/NX single/multi-page mappings, exact unmap, stale-pointer `-EFAULT`, invalid spawn pointers, malformed-ELF rejection, and three children created from user-supplied ELF bytes, followed by `-ENOMEM` at the fixed task/PID limit. Init unmaps the source image before waiting; each child verifies a zeroed two-page initial stack and exits with status 7. Wait status copyout failure returns `-EFAULT` without reaping or releasing the child root, and retry succeeds; successful wait reclaims that child's inactive root before reaping. The smoke checks all three child markers and root-reclamation markers, init exit status 42, kernel wait/reap, and final frame restoration. User-fault variants trigger #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE and a malformed syscall-return frame with `RSP = 0`; they require process exit (`128 + vector`, including status 141 for the invalid return frame), wait/reap, root teardown, and kernel survival. CPL3 #PF reads the unmapped page below the initial stack and checks CR2. NMI/#DF/#MC remain fatal; user execution is cooperative and IF-disabled with at most four concurrent processes. The bounded runtime supports nested spawn and exec but is not general-purpose userspace scheduling.

`just frame-smoke` builds an opt-in kernel variant that allocates one `Usable` frame, validates its HHDM address, writes and reads the whole page, clears it, returns it, and checks the prompt in QEMU. It reads the inherited root, walks all pages in the kernel image segments and requested 256 KiB stack span, compares effective PAT/MTRR types for kernel-image/HHDM aliases, and exercises a separate candidate map/unmap/release. The normal boot path in this image also clones the full reachable inherited hierarchy, hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while retaining PAT bits, switches CR3 with active-PCID and global-TLB invalidation, verifies the active root and critical mappings, and exercises the global heap's alignment, reuse, and deterministic exhaustion. The smoke test requires a serial marker confirming the applicable TLB invalidation path. The workflow restores the default release kernel and ISO. These probes rely on Limine's HHDM contract and do not inventory every unrelated mapping or prove physical-hardware correctness. `just fault-smoke` tests kernel-fatal page-fault, general-protection, invalid-opcode, and divide-error paths; it requires expected vector diagnostics (and CR2 for #PF), no prompt or return marker, and a halt until timeout. These fatal-path tests are distinct from `just user-fault-smoke`, which terminates a CPL3 process on #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE only when the diagnostic process runtime is installed. Diagnostic Cargo features are disabled by default and mutually exclusive, except each `probe-user-*` fault variant deliberately enables `probe-user-process`.

Keep the ACPI parser, IRQ vector allocator, PIT time arithmetic, Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, frame allocator, and fixed heap independent of hardware so ACPI signatures/checksums/MADT bounds and ACPI page-rounded span authorization, IRQ vector ownership/exhaustion, PIT divisor and elapsed-time arithmetic, syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, PAT/MTRR policy, storage semantics, frame ownership, HHDM/root-range calculations, allocation alignment, reuse, and exhaustion can be tested without booting. Pure tests validate captured MTRR register snapshots, resolve the Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR combinations for one physical address, select a PAT index that remains uniform across MTRR boundaries in an aligned range, bind that selection to validated mapping metadata before encoding leaves, and walk synthetic four-/five-level page tables including large-page leaves. Host tests also exercise process-root slot, user-mapping-record, and private-table metadata exhaustion, asserting failed operations preserve caller frame ownership and allocator accounting. They exercise the candidate builder's owned-table walk, clone ownership, 4-/5-level mapping, 2 MiB/1 GiB splitting, permission/cache-bit preservation, active-state mutation/release guard, transactional allocation/prepare rollback, retryable frame-release failure, and process preparation rollback after injected table-preparation/cache failures. Heap tests cover alignment, exact-layout free/reuse, zero-sized rejection, metadata exhaustion, and arena exhaustion. Tests reject malformed state, unsupported discontinuous masks, invalid indexes/ranges, out-of-range addresses, mismatched physical widths, and non-normal caching mode. The pure inherited-table walker does not access hardware tables; the opt-in QEMU reader and candidate backend use checked HHDM addresses. Boot-time QEMU checks a subset of live kernel/HHDM aliases but does not inventory all aliases or prove complete transition safety. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code. The temporary ACPI CR3/map/copy/restore path is hardware-only. The 2026-11-07 WSL2 q35 smoke reached the shell but rejected the MADT table span as `NotFullyAcpiBacked`; it did not validate a successful ACPI physical read or CR3 round-trip. QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

`just uefi-smoke` locates combined OVMF firmware or a matching CODE/VARS pair in standard system directories. `just thread-smoke` uses an opt-in kernel-thread probe, requires the lock-state, cooperative scheduling, non-yielding timer-preemption, and FPU-preservation markers, and restores the default release image. Split firmware uses a fresh temporary copy of the VARS template. `just input-smoke` validates UART RX and PS/2 IRQ delivery/wakeup against the normal default kernel. The OVMF checks require the expected MADT report and CR3-transition markers; install the Ubuntu `ovmf` package if no firmware is found. The BIOS smoke remains separate: if firmware places the RSDT in Reserved memory, the kernel's ACPI validation is expected to fail closed rather than accepting that table span.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test asserts the cloned CR3 transition, the applicable active-PCID/global-TLB invalidation marker, kernel HHDM alias permissions/cache preservation, heap probe, and shell prompt. The current emulator reports CR4.PGE clear; it exercises the CR3 reload path, not the PGE-toggle global flush path. `just frame-smoke` additionally exercises one allocator-owned frame, inherited paths, kernel/HHDM cache aliases, and a separate candidate mapping through Limine's HHDM contract. The clone preserves Limine's complete reachable hierarchy, but there is no clean-room mapping policy or exhaustive audit of unrelated aliases; emulator tests do not establish physical-hardware behavior. `just fault-smoke` exercises the controlled #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector or general recovery.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem test, general-purpose userspace/process-scheduler test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test. `just process-smoke` verifies bounded generation-safe slot reuse, nested child-originated spawn, exec replacement, orphan cleanup, task-capacity rejection, cooperative wait/reap, and per-child root reclamation. These tests do not establish unbounded capacity, general scheduling, SMP safety, or physical-hardware behavior.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

# Interrupts and IRQ vector allocation

## Current implementation

`src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` installs the bootstrap GDT, TSS, exception gates for vectors 0–31, device IRQ stubs, and the APIC spurious-vector gate. Kernel-origin exceptions remain fatal. The controlled Ring 3 runtime terminates noncritical CPL3 exceptions through a process callback, records status `128 + vector`, restores the kernel CR3, and exits through the user-entry trampoline. Invalid syscall return frames are also terminated as process failures rather than taking the kernel-fatal halt path. NMI (#2), double fault (#8), and machine check (#18) remain fatal regardless of saved CPL. QEMU exercises CPL3 #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE plus a syscall with an invalid saved RSP; this is not a general exception or signal mechanism. Maskable interrupts start disabled and are enabled only after the validated APIC route, registered handler, and acknowledgement path are ready.

`src/irq.rs` provides a host-tested, allocation-free token allocator for device vectors `0x20..=0xef` except reserved syscall vector `0x80`; exception vectors and the reserved upper range are also excluded. The IDT overrides `0x80` with a dedicated DPL-3 interrupt gate and assembly stub. The stub rejects CPL0 invocation, saves the full GPR set and x87/SSE state on the TSS entry stack, and dispatches a normalized syscall context with IF clear. Each entered user context owns its continuation RSP, exit status/pending flag, callback context, and kernel FXSAVE image; nested child entry restores the suspended parent's state rather than sharing global entry-depth slots. The per-entry state lets the bounded scheduler suspend one user task in wait while another runs; IF remains clear and timer preemption is not enabled for user contexts. The dispatcher implements ABI-version discovery, bounded write and wait-status copyout through allocator-owned user-frame copies, exit, wait, spawn, and exec. Spawn copies a bounded ELF image before preparation, creates a private root and guarded 1–16-page stack, and publishes the child as a cooperative task; nested spawn is covered by QEMU. Wait blocks on a process-exit queue and rechecks status after child exit. The default boot launches the bundled init, while the process and fault smokes validate fixed-capacity behavior, copyout retry, per-child root reclamation, slot/entry-stack reuse, exec replacement, and final frame restoration. User execution remains IF-disabled and bounded; this is not general-purpose process scheduling. `rustix_irq_dispatch` invokes the registered handler, returns for the APIC spurious vector without EOI, and halts on unregistered/unexpected vectors. Device handlers own their EOI. Vector registration is performed with IF clear before the corresponding I/O APIC source is unmasked.

The initial hardware target is single-vCPU QEMU `q35`: validated ACPI/MADT topology, local APIC and I/O APIC, masked legacy PIC routing, MADT-resolved ISA routes, and a periodic 8254 PIT tick near 100 Hz. OVMF smokes validate PIT delivery/EOI, non-yielding timer preemption, x87/SSE state preservation, and UART/keyboard IRQ delivery. Host tests cover vector ownership and PIT/time arithmetic; they do not replace privileged QEMU coverage.

The scheduler is single-vCPU and supports cooperative waits/yields plus PIT-driven timer preemption. The timer handler advances ticks and sends APIC EOI before any scheduling switch. The common IRQ stub saves the interrupted x87/SSE state before Rust dispatch and restores the selected context before `IRETQ`; the context switch keeps aligned per-context FXSAVE areas. IRQ-safe spin locks save and restore the prior IF state, and the global heap uses one; scheduler mutations are separately serialized by masking local interrupts. IRQ/exception handlers remain bounded and allocation-free, and no current IRQ handler acquires the heap lock. SMP, per-CPU state, and physical-hardware validation remain future work.

# Memory-management direction

## What exists now

`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, HHDM range arithmetic, and page-rounded ACPI span authorization. `MemoryMap::validate_acpi_span` accepts at most 64 KiB of requested ACPI bytes and validates the entire 4 KiB-rounded physical extent against contiguous ACPI-reclaimable/NVS regions; this is metadata only, not a mapping or dereference grant. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.

`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The boot path additionally subtracts the validated kernel-image and boot-stack physical spans (`from_memory_map_excluding`) so a loader mislabeling them as usable cannot cause the allocator to hand out own-kernel pages. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. The active cloned page-table hierarchy owns its page-table frames; the frame allocator is otherwise not yet a general-purpose virtual-memory service.

`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.

`src/paging.rs` contains host-tested mapping and cache policy plus a bounded candidate-root builder. The CR3 decoder validates physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets its low 12 bits according to active `CR4.PCIDE`; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires known physical width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. It can encode one 4 KiB leaf PTE with supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when EFER.NXE is confirmed, and a bounded PAT index. `PatLayout` parses supplied `IA32_PAT` values and selects WB, UC, or WC indexes. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve address-specific MTRR types, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` validates captured capability/default-type bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, and variable-mask shape/alignment before producing an owned layout. Rustix supports contiguous power-of-two variable masks and explicitly rejects unsupported discontinuous masks. The layout combines address-specific MTRR type and PAT selection according to Intel SDM Table 11-7 only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT pairs and malformed inputs. A pure range selector chooses an index only when its effective type is uniform throughout all fixed/variable MTRR boundaries in an aligned extent; selected attributes remain bound to that physical extent. The selector itself does not inspect PTEs, aliases, or frame ownership. Boot reads CR0 without modifying it, validates captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic PA 0 resolution; this does not assert the live PTE's type. MTRR capture is bounded to 32 variable pairs and rejects excess capacity without partial state.

`CandidatePageTables` owns a separate root, bounded to 32 table frames and 256 explicitly mapped leaf records. Ordinary owned leaves require allocator-issued `Frame` tokens; a separate bounded ACPI path accepts only one read-only, supervisor, NX 4 KiB page contained in a `ValidatedAcpiSpan` and never transfers ownership of that physical page. Both paths require NXE, support four- and five-level paths, and hold one exclusive mutable borrow of the unsafe memory backend so prepared handles cannot be mixed across backends. Borrowed ACPI mappings can only be installed and removed while the candidate is inactive. The boot-only ACPI reader performs temporary CR3 switches to read validated pages and removes them before permanent activation. The default boot path clones the complete reachable Limine hierarchy, hardens kernel HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while preserving PAT bits, verifies critical translations, activates the cloned CR3, and retains the candidate tokens for the active root's lifetime. The CR3 transition invalidates the active PCID and toggles CR4.PGE when enabled; the same invalidation is used if verification restores the inherited root. General candidate mutation and release are rejected while active, but narrow owned-page active map/unmap operations are supported under the single-CPU, IF-disabled contract and invalidate the local TLB before ownership is returned. Host tests cover transactional rollback and ownership; `just active-map-smoke` validates active mapping, access, invalidation, and reclamation in QEMU. The type never writes CR3. The HHDM adapter derives table pointers only from complete allocator-owned `Usable` frames through checked arithmetic.

The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe reads the inherited root and follows paths for every page in kernel text/rodata/data and the requested stack span. The transition clones every reachable present table and preserves leaf mappings, then rewrites and validates the kernel-image HHDM aliases. The kernel and HHDM aliases retain the same PAT index; MTRR state is unchanged. This is not a fresh address-space policy or a hardware-level exhaustive inventory, and it does not reclaim the inherited root or bootloader memory.

The effective-type resolver follows [Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.5.2.2, Table 11-7](https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/671447/325384-sdm-vol-3abcd.pdf), which applies when normal caching is enabled (`CR0.CD=0`, `CR0.NW=0`). Its footnotes distinguish UC selected by an MTRR from UC selected by a page-table entry (the latter involves cache snooping and aliasing concerns); they also identify combinations that older manual editions called undefined but current processors supporting both PAT and MTRRs resolve as shown. The resolver does not cover legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations outside that table.

The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. Limine's inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Before activating the cloned root, Rustix splits inherited huge pages where needed and changes the kernel image HHDM aliases to the matching R/NX or RW/NX policy while retaining PAT bits. The rest of the HHDM remains inherited; an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.

The boot snapshot rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when available. For base-revision-3 HHDM-mapped types it validates page-rounded physical spans, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. These checks are metadata, not proof that loader pointers are readable. Arbitrary physical access is not permitted: validated ACPI pages use the bounded read-only/NX reader; HHDM table access is limited to checked full-frame paths. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. The APIC MMIO validator rejects every known memory-map class except `Reserved` and `Unknown`; unreported ranges remain dependent on validated platform data. The active clone owns its page-table frames but leaves inherited leaf frames and the old root unreclaimed. The global heap begins with a 256 KiB BSS arena and can demand-map up to 1 MiB of allocator-backed pages in its reserved virtual range. Its IRQ-save lock prevents local interrupt reentrancy, but allocation remains forbidden in IRQ/exception handlers. Bootstrap exceptions remain fatal, while selected maskable IRQs are enabled only after APIC routes and handlers are ready.

## Active-root preservation and remaining limits

The transition clones the complete reachable inherited hierarchy rather than building a clean address space. It preserves all reachable present leaves and non-present entries, owns each cloned intermediate table, and fails closed on malformed entries, unsupported page sizes, cross-level table aliases, or fixed-capacity exhaustion. Kernel text/rodata/data HHDM aliases are then adjusted to avoid writable-executable aliases. Limine's original root and leaf frames remain intact.

- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. Rustix requests a 256 KiB Limine stack and requires the stack-size response; `BootInfo` records and validates that requested span through the HHDM, including its `BootloaderReclaimable` backing. The loader may allocate more, and no guard page is inferred. QEMU transition tests walk all 64 requested stack pages.
- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates the decoded root address and active low-bit mode. The default boot path clones all reachable page-table pages into allocator-owned frames and preserves all leaf entries, then changes only the kernel-image HHDM alias permission bits while retaining cache attributes. It verifies kernel segments, the requested stack span, and the candidate-root HHDM alias before switching; afterward it verifies CR3 and the critical paths again. The inherited root and its backing pages remain untouched and are not reclaimed.
- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.

## Permissions and cache policy of the active clone

The active root preserves Limine's inherited kernel virtual mappings and their cache attributes. Before switching, Rustix requires NXE and enforces the linker permissions for every kernel-image HHDM alias: text and rodata are read-only/NX, and data/BSS/GOT are RW/NX. This prevents writable-executable aliases without discarding the HHDM alias. Huge-page leaves are split as necessary; unaffected entries retain their mappings and PAT/MTRR effective types. The remainder of the HHDM and all non-kernel aliases remain as Limine supplied them, so this is not yet a comprehensive Rustix mapping policy.

Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The boot report validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching. A separate pure selector can choose an index whose effective type remains uniform across an aligned physical range; the selector itself does not inspect PTEs or aliases. The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe now compares effective types of the inherited kernel and HHDM aliases for kernel-image pages, but it is not a full alias inventory. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations. The active transition retains the inherited PAT and MTRR state and changes no cache-selection bits. The page-table split copies large-page PAT selection to the equivalent 4 KiB/2 MiB entries. Future MMIO mappings must still use explicit device ranges and a verified cache policy; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.

Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.

Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. `src/paging.rs` builds an owned clone in allocator-issued frames, can split inherited large pages to update leaf permissions, and supports transactional 4 KiB map/unmap operations before activation. The default boot path validates critical translations and kernel alias permissions, switches CR3 while invalidating stale global translations via a CR4.PGE toggle when needed, verifies the active root, and retains its frame tokens for the active lifetime. The inherited root and backing memory remain intact. This preserves inherited mappings rather than constructing a new address space; broader mapping inventory, non-kernel permission policy, reclamation, and a general mapping service remain future work.

## Planned memory layers

1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; table and leaf mappings use allocator-issued tokens. The active mapping smoke validates one owned page's map/access/unmap/reclamation path.
3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix runs on an active clone of Limine's hierarchy and hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases. Narrow active owned-page map/unmap operations invalidate the local TLB; this is not a clean-room address-space policy or general MMIO subsystem.
4. **Heap:** a 256 KiB BSS arena with 128 allocation records is backed by a bounded, demand-mapped extension of up to 1 MiB. Host tests and QEMU cover growth, reuse, exhaustion, and failed growth. The global allocator uses an IRQ-save spin lock, but allocation remains prohibited in interrupt context so handlers stay bounded and allocation-free.
5. **Process address spaces (partial):** `SharedKernelHalf` validates/snapshots the upper root entries, and `ProcessAddressSpaceRoots` constructs multiple private roots, maps lower-half user leaves from allocator-issued frames, returns ownership on unmap, and frees private mappings/tables/root during inactive teardown. The view borrows the kernel-root owner, which must remain alive and immutable; the root set uses one exclusive backend borrow for its roots. `destroy` is permitted only after the caller switches away and invalidates the root's local non-global translations; PCID-aware teardown is unsupported. The caller still owns CR3 transitions. Mapping metadata retains writable and executable permissions, and `validate_initial_user_state` requires an executable non-writable entry page plus a writable non-executable stack page. Generic copy-in/copy-out helpers preflight lower-half mapped ranges and permissions and access owned frames through a separate `UserFrameMemory` contract. `Elf64Image::load_into_process_root` allocates, populates, cache-selects, and maps bounded ELF load pages. Default boot loads the bundled init ELF into a private process root; process-smoke additionally exercises separate child ELFs in independent roots. Init runs with token-based write/EFAULT handling; its wait cooperatively blocks the scheduler task on a process-exit queue while the kernel-prepared child runs, then resumes after child exit and copies status before reaping. The kernel harness later waits/reaps init and tears down both inactive roots. Its one-page initial stack is cleared in bounded chunks before mapping, and Ring 3 checks an untouched byte is zero. It has an unmapped page immediately below it; startup checks that page is unmapped, and `just user-fault-smoke` reads it from CPL3 and checks the resulting #PF CR2 before validating teardown. A fixed-capacity `UserRegionTable` reserves the ELF segments, stack, and guard, and provides first-fit page-rounded anonymous-region reservations within a bounded lower-half window. The opt-in process probe exposes one-page `mmap`/`munmap` calls: it zeroes RW/NX frames before mapping, switches to the kernel root for PTE changes, and only releases a frame after unmapping it. QEMU verifies a fresh mapped page, user write/read, stale-address EFAULT after unmap, and root teardown. This is still a bounded one-page-per-call VM interface, not stack growth or a general userspace memory manager. `just process-smoke` validates actual child entry/exit, blocking wait, EFAULT copyout retry, and root/frame teardown. This remains a bounded cooperative process service, not general-purpose userspace. Any active process may spawn from copied user ELF bytes; four total process slots bound concurrency. Successful wait reclaims each inactive child root only after status copyout succeeds, while failed copyout leaves it waitable. The runtime supports nested spawn and exec; default boot launches the controlled init. Dynamic stack growth, unbounded capacity, a curated kernel map, SMP shootdown, and complete fault recovery remain future work. The process smoke validates three spawned children, fixed task-capacity rejection, per-child root reclamation after successful wait, and scheduler-owned guarded kernel-task stack reclamation after the bounded task set exits.

`process::prepare_user_program` is the reusable static-image preparation layer: it creates a fresh private root, loads validated ELF segments, reserves an unmapped guard, maps a zero-filled RW/NX stack of 1–16 pages, and validates the initial user entry/IRET frame. Failures clean up transactionally where possible; any root or unattached frame that cannot be reclaimed is returned in a must-use error with a retryable `cleanup` method. The default init launch and syscall spawn/exec paths use this API; scheduler and process lifecycle remain bounded to the single-vCPU runtime. Host tests verify multi-page stack zeroing and rollback after injected table-preparation/cache-policy failures and at every remaining-frame budget below successful preparation; separate process-root tests fill root, mapping-record, and private-table metadata capacities and verify failed mappings return the leaf token without changing allocator accounting. The `CandidatePageTableMemory` contract currently treats individual `write_entry` operations as infallible, so tests cannot inject a write failure mid-PTE transaction.

## Invariants to preserve

- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. HHDM translation and table access are limited to checked full-frame token-based paths that rely on Limine's documented mapping contract. Candidate mutations are allowed only before activation and only in owned tables. The active cloned root retains its ownership tokens and rejects mutation/release until an explicit, reviewed CR3 transition away from it.
- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables. User-accessible leaf mappings must stay in the lower canonical half; the upper half is reserved for supervisor mappings.
- User-controlled addresses are validated on every syscall boundary; prior validation is not a substitute for access checks during later copies.
- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.

The active root is a full clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy with kernel HHDM alias W^X hardening, not a clean-room Rustix address space. Heap growth is bounded to a fixed virtual reservation and 1 MiB of frame-backed pages. Broader alias/MMIO coverage, frame reclamation, and physical-hardware validation remain outstanding.

It decodes CR3's physical root address and low-bit meaning against those CPU properties, without dereferencing the root. Single-vCPU timer preemption is implemented with IRQ-safe locking and validated context switching; SMP still requires separately designed per-CPU and synchronization rules. The controlled Ring 3 runtime terminates noncritical CPL3 exceptions through a process callback, records status `128 + vector`, restores the kernel CR3, and exits through the user-entry trampoline. Invalid syscall return frames are also terminated as process failures rather than taking the kernel-fatal halt path. NMI (#2), double fault (#8), and machine check (#18) remain fatal regardless of saved CPL. QEMU exercises CPL3 #PF/#GP/#UD/#DE plus a syscall with an invalid saved RSP; this is not a general exception or signal mechanism.
